Use MCP HTTP with tenant-scoped tools/list and resources/list results, bind the client to its tenant and scopes, and recheck authorization on read and invocation.
Use MCP for transport but bind all sessions to a shared tenant role because the server has one deployment.

prompt:
Four remote clients use a shared MCP server over HTTP. Each tenant has distinct read and write scopes. The server declares support for tools and resources, but its tools/list and resources/list responses expose entries to a client from the wrong tenant. Policy prohibits showing operations or resources the client cannot access.

Which protocol and authorization boundary should the shared HTTP server implement?

constraints: Multiple clients need one typed lifecycle and capability protocol.
Servers should evolve independently while clients discover supported capabilities.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protocol adoption adds implementation and versioning work, but it removes duplicated schemas and gives clients a common capability boundary.
details.errorCorrection: Choose an integration mechanism from interoperability and lifecycle requirements, not from the fact that every client can call an HTTP endpoint.
details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP uses a JSON-RPC client-server interaction with initialization and capability negotiation, and can expose tools, resources, and prompts through the protocol.
details.scenarioApplication: Approved servers advertise supported capabilities and clients invoke typed tools or read resources through the common contract while each server evolves independently.
details.transfer: Use a shared protocol when several clients need typed discovery and independently managed capability servers; use a narrower direct interface for one deterministic caller.

messages.text: Private wrappers duplicate schemas and lifecycle behavior across languages and make capability evolution inconsistent.
OpenAPI or JSON Schema can type operations, but per-client lifecycle and discovery conventions do not provide the requested shared MCP negotiation for resources and prompts.
Per-language SDKs can be typed, but they duplicate lifecycle and capability behavior and make independently evolving servers harder to consume consistently.

feedback.reason: The requirements call for a shared typed protocol with lifecycle and capability negotiation across clients and servers. MCP provides that integration surface without duplicating private wrappers.

options.text: Copy private HTTP wrappers and schemas into each client so every language can tailor its integration independently.
Use a shared OpenAPI or JSON Schema catalog for typed operations, while each client implements its own lifecycle, resource, prompt, and capability-negotiation conventions.
Use MCP with clients and servers implementing the JSON-RPC lifecycle and relevant capability negotiation, tools, resources, and prompts.
Publish typed SDK bindings for each language and version them alongside the servers, with clients maintaining their own resource and prompt discovery behavior.

prompt: An organization wants one integration surface for several Claude clients written in different languages. It needs typed tools, resources, prompts, capability negotiation, and independently evolving approved servers. Which mechanism fits?

constraints: Workers need scoped objectives, source guidance, and structured handoffs.
One lead owns synthesis; a tool protocol alone does not define research coordination.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Agent coordination adds state, artifacts, and lead synthesis cost, but it reduces duplicated context and makes source responsibility explicit.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish a protocol for calling tools from a coordination contract for independent agents and their final owner.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Workers receive bounded assignments and return structured artifacts, while a lead agent coordinates and synthesizes those artifacts after retrieval and source checks.
details.scenarioApplication: Assign one market question per worker, require source and uncertainty fields, and join each artifact to the lead report and its citations.
details.transfer: For open-ended specialist work, define worker objectives and evidence handoffs, then preserve ownership through final synthesis.

messages.text: MCP may expose tools but does not assign research objectives, ownership, or synthesis responsibilities.
Full-history independent reports waste context and make conflict and source ownership harder for the lead to resolve.
One response hides independent failure and ownership boundaries and cannot provide the requested worker handoffs.
Without explicit agent objectives and structured assignments, workers cannot be coordinated or evaluated as independent research units.
Without preserved ownership and evidence identifiers, the lead cannot attribute or reconcile conflicting findings.

feedback.reason: The workload is independent research with explicit ownership and a synthesis lead. Agent-to-agent coordination supplies objectives and handoffs; preserving ownership and evidence lets the lead reconcile rather than guess.

options.text: Use MCP as the only coordination mechanism and let workers infer their objectives from the available tools.
Use agent-to-agent orchestration with explicit worker objectives, source and output guidance, bounded assignments, and structured artifacts for the lead.
Give every worker the full conversation and ask each to return a complete final report for the lead to choose by prose quality.
Run one shared API call for all markets and let Claude simulate specialist ownership inside a single response.
Preserve worker ownership and evidence identifiers in each handoff so the lead can reconcile conflicts and cite the responsible source.

prompt: A research lead delegates independent market questions to specialist workers. Each worker searches different sources and returns structured evidence; the lead synthesizes one report with explicit ownership. Which TWO integration decisions fit? Select TWO.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If metadata were intentionally public under an explicit policy, global discovery could be allowed while private calls and reads remained protected.
details.errorCorrection: Titles and names have already crossed the metadata boundary before invocation. A feature declaration change does not repair leaking discovery responses. Post-response hiding cannot undo disclosure to the client and is not server-side authorization.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Call/read denial protects execution but not discovery metadata. This policy requires tenant-scoped list responses as well as access checks on subsequent operations.
details.scenarioApplication: Bind discovery to the authenticated client, filter both list methods, and recheck the same resource permissions at use time.
details.transfer: Enforce each policy at the earliest boundary where the protected information could be disclosed.

messages.text: Titles and names have already crossed the metadata boundary before invocation.
A feature declaration change does not repair leaking discovery responses.
Post-response hiding cannot undo disclosure to the client and is not server-side authorization.

feedback.reason: Call/read denial protects execution but not discovery metadata. This policy requires tenant-scoped list responses as well as access checks on subsequent operations.

options.text: Filter discovery entries by authenticated tenant and scopes while retaining authorization checks on calls and reads.
Keep the lists because invocation-time denial prevents every kind of leak.
Remove the resources capability declaration but keep returning private entries.
Let the model hide forbidden titles after the server returns them.

prompt: A shared MCP server declares support for tools and resources. A tenant-A client receives a tools/list response containing tenant-B tool names and resources/list entries revealing tenant-B document titles. Calls and reads are correctly denied. Policy prohibits cross-tenant metadata disclosure. What must change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the policy prohibited exposing inaccessible operation names, discovery would also need filtering, as well as call-time enforcement.
details.errorCorrection: A listed schema describes an available operation; it does not grant invocation permission. The explicit policy permits public metadata; no private metadata disclosure is stated. A shared role would bypass the required tenant and scope isolation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Public discovery and protected invocation are separate policy decisions. The tool name can be visible while tools/call rejects missing write scope.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain the intentionally public catalogue and deny the write operation before any side effect or tenant-data access.
details.transfer: A discovered capability is not a delegated permission; enforce the actual metadata and execution policies separately.

messages.text: A listed schema describes an available operation; it does not grant invocation permission.
The explicit policy permits public metadata; no private metadata disclosure is stated.
A shared role would bypass the required tenant and scope isolation.

feedback.reason: Public discovery and protected invocation are separate policy decisions. The tool name can be visible while tools/call rejects missing write scope.

options.text: Grant write scope because discovery is proof of authorization.
Reject the call for missing write scope; the public discovery response remains permitted by policy.
Declare the whole server noncompliant solely because a public tool name was listed.
Execute the call under a shared server role without the client tenant binding.

prompt: An MCP service intentionally publishes a global catalogue of non-sensitive tool names and schemas. Policy allows every authenticated tenant to discover this public metadata, but tools/call must enforce tenant-specific scopes and data isolation. A tenant without write scope can list a write tool. What should happen when it tries to call that tool?
